text: A stateful firewall tracks the state of every active connection in a state table, remembering which connections are currently open and what reply traffic to expect back. A stateless firewall keeps no memory of anything at all — it judges every single packet in isolation against a fixed set of rules. That one difference changes almost everything about how each type of firewall actually behaves on real traffic.

Say a laptop opens a connection out to 203.0.113.10 on port 443 for HTTPS. The stateful firewall immediately logs that connection in its state table. When the reply packets arrive a moment later, the firewall checks them against the table, finds a matching established connection, and passes them through automatically — no separate inbound rule required. An unrelated packet claiming to be a reply, with no matching entry in the table, gets dropped outright, because nothing on the inside ever requested it.

A stateless firewall has no such memory to lean on. Every packet is evaluated entirely on its own against static rules covering source address, destination address, port, and protocol, with no concept of an already-approved conversation in progress. To let legitimate reply traffic back in at all, an administrator has to write an explicit rule permitting it — which makes stateless rule sets tedious to get right, and easy to make either too permissive or too restrictive.

Maintaining a state table isn't free — it costs real CPU and memory, especially on a device handling a very large number of simultaneous connections at once. Stateless filtering skips all of that bookkeeping entirely, judging each packet cheaply and fast, at the real cost of understanding almost nothing about the traffic. Stateful is smarter but heavier on resources; stateless is cheap and fast but fundamentally dumb about what it actually lets through.

In practice, most modern firewalls are stateful by default, because the security benefit of understanding connections usually outweighs the resource cost on today's hardware. Stateless filtering still earns a place on resource-constrained devices and as a fast first filtering pass before traffic ever reaches a stateful device. Next up: next-generation firewalls and deep packet inspection — looking inside the actual payload, not just the headers, to see what kind of traffic is really passing through.
